name: Basics
description: Warm up the muscles every later topic assumes: loops, arithmetic on digits, a first taste of recursion, and the hash map you will reach for hundreds of times from here on.

name: Sorting
description: Write the classic sorts by hand once so the loop invariants stick, then learn the far more common skill: choosing the key that makes a problem trivial to sort into an answer.

name: Arrays
description: The workhorse topic. Forty problems taking you from one-pass scans and hash lookups through in-place matrix surgery and interval merging, up to the hard counting problems that need a modified merge sort.

name: Binary Search
description: Binary search is not really about sorted arrays; it is about monotone predicates. Start on plain arrays, then learn to search the space of possible answers, then take it into two dimensions.

name: Strings
description: Strings are arrays with a bounded alphabet, which opens doors arrays do not have: counting arrays, rolling hashes and prefix functions. Start with careful case analysis, finish with parsing.

name: Linked Lists
description: Pointer discipline. A dummy head, a saved next pointer and a drawing on paper solve most of these — then the fast and slow pointer trick solves the rest in constant space.

name: Recursion
description: Learn to trust the recursive call. These problems separate the two halves of recursive thinking: defining what the function promises, and handling only the current step.

name: Backtracking
description: Systematic search with an undo button. Three questions define every problem here: what is a choice, what makes it legal, and when is the answer complete.

name: Bit Manipulation
description: A small toolbox with outsized reach: clearing the lowest set bit, isolating it, and the fact that XOR cancels duplicates. Write the binary out by hand for the first few cases.

name: Stack and Queue
description: Two structures, one big idea each: the stack remembers what is still unresolved, and the monotonic variant of it answers every "nearest greater element" question in linear time.

name: Sliding Window and Two Pointers
description: Two techniques that turn quadratic double loops into linear sweeps. The two-pointer version needs an ordering; the sliding-window version needs a monotone validity condition.

name: Heaps
description: A heap gives you the extreme element cheaply without paying for a full sort. The counter-intuitive bit — a min-heap for the k largest — is worth internalising early.

name: Greedy Algorithms
description: Commit to the locally best choice and never look back. The technique is easy; knowing when it is actually correct is the skill, so try to break each rule before you trust it.

name: Binary Trees
description: Thirty-nine problems that all reduce to one question: what does each child report upward, and what does the parent pass down? Get that right and the code is five lines.

name: Binary Search Trees
description: Add an ordering to a binary tree and traversal becomes search. The inorder sequence being sorted is the fact that solves most of these.

name: Graphs
description: The biggest topic on the ladder, and the one that pays back most. Fifty-four problems from grid flood fills through topological ordering and the four shortest-path algorithms, up to bridges and strongly connected components.

name: Dynamic Programming
description: The largest topic, ordered so each family builds on the last. Every problem here follows the same route: recursion, memoisation, tabulation, then space optimisation. Define the state precisely and the rest follows.

name: Tries
description: A tree where the path spells the key. Small topic, but it is the structure behind autocomplete, and its binary form turns maximum-XOR queries into a greedy walk.

name: Advanced Data Structures and Algorithms
description: The last rung. Range-query structures, offline processing and a few designs that show up in senior interviews. Attempt these once the rest of the ladder is comfortable.
